G1.rationale: The principal result is a computed proportion/effect from survey data using a linear probability model; a third party can re-run the computation on the deposited data.

quotes.quote: However, when other countries are merely mentioned to also introduce a carbon tax, support is 59%, which is equivalent to a 6 percentage points increase over the unilateralism condition.
In the control condition that did not receive any effectiveness information, we find that about 53% of all respondents support the introduction of a carbon tax if this policy is pursued unilaterally.

G2.rationale: The paper's stated principal result is the effect of multilateralism on carbon tax support; the first reported numerical endpoint is the 6 percentage point increase (53% to 59%).

quotes.quote: The data used in this study are available at the Harvard Dataverse as Bechtel, Michael; Scheve, Kenneth; van Lieshout, Elisabeth, 2022, “Replication Data for: Improving Public Support for Climate Action Through Multilateralism”, 10.7910/DVN/GCNO77, Harvard Dataverse, V1.

G3.rationale: The deposit contains pooled_scenlevel_touse.dta and pooled_touse.tab, which are the analysis input data files; the .do/.R files are code, not inputs.

G4.rationale: The outcome definition, model type, controls, fixed effects, and weighting are described sufficiently to implement without the original code.

quotes.quote: The following software has been used to process the data: Excel (MacOS 16.65), Stata 16, and R.

G5.rationale: The method can be implemented in R or other free software; no proprietary software is required for the statistical computation.

specification.exact_target: The effect of multilateralism on carbon tax support in the control condition: support is 53% under unilateralism and 59% under multilateralism, a 6 percentage point increase.
specification.blind_target: The difference in the proportion of respondents approving a domestic carbon tax between a multilateral and a unilateral policy framing, in the condition without additional effectiveness information.

location_quotes.quote: In the control condition that did not receive any effectiveness information, we find that about 53% of all respondents support the introduction of a carbon tax if this policy is pursued unilaterally.
However, when other countries are merely mentioned to also introduce a carbon tax, support is 59%, which is equivalent to a 6 percentage points increase over the unilateralism condition.

method_quotes.quote: We analyze the proportion of individuals approving the introduction of a carbon tax (levels of support that exceed 5, the midpoint of the scale).
estimated using a linear probability model with robust standard errors. Regressions control for gender, age, income, education, and employment status. Country fixed effects included.
All our results employ survey weights, but the findings are very similar when analyzing the unweighted data.

specification.input_notes: The deposit is Harvard Dataverse GCNO77 V1. The .dta and .tab files are the pooled analysis datasets; the .do and .R files are original code and are withheld. No external data are needed.

specification.comparison_metric: Compare the reported proportions (53% and 59%) and their difference (6 percentage points) to the solver's computed weighted proportions and difference from the deposited data.
specification.numerical_agreement_criterion: Proportions by numerator/denominator within the displayed rounding bin (whole percentage points); the difference must equal the reported 6 percentage points within rounding.
specification.specification_gaps: The exact survey weight variable, the precise coding of the 1–10 approval scale into a binary indicator, and the exact model specification for the control-condition proportion are not fully specified in the text.

alternatives_considered.target: The 6 percentage point increase in the high effectiveness condition (57% to 62%)
alternatives_considered.reason: This is a secondary mechanism result, not the principal first-reported effect.

alternatives_considered.target: The conjoint cost effects (e.g., 6 and 17 percentage point drops)
alternatives_considered.reason: These are from the second study and are not the paper's principal first-reported result.
